source.title: When Does Preconditioning Help or Hurt Generalization?
source.authors: S. Amari; Jimmy Ba; R. Grosse; Xuechen Li; Atsushi Nitanda; Taiji Suzuki; Denny Wu; Ji Xu

record.tranche_reason: Compares preconditioned gradient descent, especially natural gradient descent (NGD), with ordinary gradient descent (GD) using population risk; this is a conceptual test of optimizer effects on generalization, not the adaptive-optimizer benchmarks in V4.
record.gate_note: The study tests GD versus NGD across noise, misspecification, signal alignment, and preconditioner settings. It does not test memorization of random labels, network width, convolutional versus fully connected architectures, batch size, dropout, sharpness measures, or removal of memorized examples. Cited optimizer comparisons are not extracted as results.
record.test_reason: The study compares GD with population-Fisher NGD and related preconditioners in regression. V4 concerns adaptive optimizers such as Adam under specified tuning regimes; the authors explicitly exclude these methods from their theoretical coverage. The study cites adaptive-optimizer comparisons but supplies no direct test of V4 or any other listed version.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. The authors find that noise, misspecification, signal alignment, and population versus sample Fisher information affect GD–NGD generalization comparisons. Interpolation and early stopping can alter the comparison. They also prove accelerated population-risk convergence in an RKHS setting, caution against assuming transfer to neural networks, and explicitly leave many adaptive gradient methods outside their analysis.
record.recipe_differences: Compares GD with population-Fisher NGD and interpolations in student-teacher regression experiments and theoretical ridgeless regression; it does not reproduce the adaptive-optimizer benchmark recipes in V4.
record.method_sensitivity: The comparison changes with label-noise level, teacher pretraining/misspecification, signal alignment, number of unlabeled examples used to estimate the Fisher, and preconditioner interpolation/damping.

fits_no_version.finding: Population-Fisher NGD minimizes stationary variance; GD minimizes bias for isotropic signal, while NGD can have lower bias for misaligned signal. Independent unobserved features contribute variance-like misspecified bias.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The generalization comparison between GD and population-Fisher NGD depends on noise, misspecification, and signal alignment.

fits_no_version.finding: Fewer Fisher-estimation examples make NGD risk more similar to GD; intermediate preconditioners can improve stationary risk at some noise levels.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Fisher estimation and interpolation between GD and NGD affect the bias–variance tradeoff.

fits_no_version.finding: GD produces smaller parameter changes, population-Fisher NGD smaller function changes, and sample-Fisher NGD resembles GD.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Population- and sample-Fisher preconditioning can impose different implicit biases.

record.problems: Neural-network experiments use a student-teacher distillation setup and test error as a proxy for stationary risk. Figures generally provide trends rather than tabulated values. Experiments report five independent runs for Figure 8, but several later comparisons provide no uncertainty in the text. The authors caution that linear and kernel conclusions do not always transfer to neural networks and that the misalignment analogy is superficial.
record.rows_left_out: No additional rows beyond R1–R11. Figure 14 reports a heuristic NTK-based misspecification measure, not generalization performance, so it is not a row for V4.

untested.parts: Fixed random-label fitting versus natural-label classification generalization using the same architecture and recipe.
Network widening beyond zero training error. Linear-regression feature-to-sample ratios and their nonmonotonic risks do not measure network width.
Matched convolutional versus fully connected classifiers and the contribution of local connectivity.
Adaptive versus SGD optimizers under limited or broader tuning, including switching, weight decay, and language-model conditions. Adam is used only for teacher pretraining.
Large versus small training batches under fixed epoch budgets and adapted recipes.
Dropout comparisons, small-data and underfitting regimes, and joint removal of dropout and weight decay.
Magnitude-aware perturbation sharpness, its association with generalization gaps, and ranking against alternative measures.
Removing highly memorized examples versus equally many random examples and retraining.

record.verdict_notes: The record's V4 limits_scope verdict should be removed: related second-order optimizer results do not qualify the specified adaptive-optimizer claim. Appendix C.3 additionally reports that early stopping favors GD across the tested CIFAR-10 noise levels, but this also fits no listed version. No missing results bearing directly on V1–V8 were identified.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label memorization and generalization on natural labels.
Width sweeps beyond the interpolation threshold.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers.
Adam and other adaptive optimizers; language benchmarks; equal training performance; limited versus broader tuning; decoupled weight decay; switching optimizers; weight decay effects.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and comparisons with norm- and margin-based measures.
Removing memorized training examples and measuring test accuracy.

rows.subject: GD
rows.operation_detail: Theoretical stationary variance of the ridgeless interpolant under identity preconditioning.
rows.measure: Stationary variance component of population risk.
rows.baseline: NGD stationary variance lower bound: σ²(γ − 1)⁻¹
rows.value: V(θ̂P) ≥ σ²(γ − 1)⁻¹; equality when P = F⁻¹ = ΣX⁻¹ (NGD).
rows.note: GD uses P = I; the result states NGD attains the minimum variance, so this comparison does not support a general claim that preconditioning worsens held-out performance.
rows.check: Theorem 1 concerns all admissible preconditioners, with NGD attaining minimum stationary variance; GD is one comparator. This variance component does not measure V4's adaptive-optimizer comparison.

rows.subject: GD
rows.operation_detail: Theoretical comparison of stationary bias for a well-specified linear teacher with isotropic parameter prior.
rows.measure: Stationary bias component of population risk.
rows.value: GD achieves lower bias than NGD when the true parameters have roughly equal magnitude (isotropic).
rows.note: Bias is one component of population risk; the result does not alone establish which optimizer has lower total risk.
rows.check: Correctly describes GD's lower stationary bias under isotropic signal, but measures neither adaptive optimizers nor total held-out performance.

rows.subject: GD
rows.operation_detail: Theoretical comparison of stationary bias for a well-specified linear teacher with misaligned signal.
rows.measure: Stationary bias component of population risk.
rows.value: NGD achieves lower bias when the target focuses on small feature directions; Figure 6(c) uses Σθ = ΣX⁻¹.
rows.note: Bias is one component of population risk.
rows.check: Correctly describes NGD's lower stationary bias under misalignment; this does not establish a reversal of V4.

rows.subject: GD
rows.operation_detail: Theoretical comparison of risk under misspecification represented by independent unobserved linear features.

conditions.value: misspecification contributes additional bias analogous to variance

rows.measure: Additional bias due to misspecification and stationary variance.
rows.value: The additional misspecified bias is proportional to V(θ̂P) + 1; NGD is optimal for the variance term.
rows.note: The paper says it expects the characterization to hold more broadly; the stated corollary is for the specified unobserved-features model.
rows.check: The corollary concerns the additional misspecified bias component, not necessarily total risk. It does not test adaptive optimizers.

rows.subject: GD
rows.operation_detail: Trained student with GD or NGD on teacher labels corrupted by isotropic Gaussian noise; reported test error as a proxy for stationary risk.

conditions.value: two-layer ReLU network with 80 hidden units

rows.value: As noise increases, stationary risk worsens for both, with GD worsening faster.
rows.uncertainty: Error bar is one standard deviation over five independent runs.
rows.note: Figure 8(a) reports a trend, not tabulated numeric values.
rows.check: The result compares GD and NGD on regression to teacher logits. Test error denotes prediction risk, not image-classification error; neither optimizer comparison tests V4.

rows.subject: two-layer ReLU student; ResNet-20 teacher
rows.stage_stated: student distilled from teacher; teacher pretraining varied
rows.operation_detail: Trained the same student setup with GD or NGD using labels from teachers with varying pretraining.
rows.value: NGD eventually achieves better generalization as the number of teacher training steps increases.
rows.uncertainty: Error bar is one standard deviation over five independent runs.
rows.note: The reported advantage appears as teacher pretraining increases; the figure does not provide tabulated values.
rows.check: The NGD advantage with longer teacher pretraining concerns teacher-logit regression, not adaptive-optimizer classification performance. The student has 80 hidden units under the stated shared setup.

rows.subject: two-layer ReLU student and teacher
rows.size_stated: two-layer ReLU network; width not stated for this experiment
rows.stage_stated: student and teacher share architecture; teacher initialized by perturbing student initialization
rows.operation_detail: Compared GD and NGD while varying the teacher perturbation direction using powers of the student Fisher.

conditions.value: r ∈ [−1, 0]; smaller r is more misaligned

rows.value: As r becomes smaller (more misaligned), NGD begins to generalize better than GD.
rows.uncertainty: Error bar is one standard deviation over five independent runs.
rows.note: The authors describe the analogy as superficial because of neural-network nonconvexity.
rows.check: Manipulated teacher alignment changes the GD–NGD regression comparison, outside V4. Figure 8(c) specifies 60000 unlabeled examples for Fisher estimation.

rows.subject: two-layer ReLU student
rows.size_stated: two-layer; width not stated for this experiment
rows.operation_detail: Varied the number of unlabeled examples used to estimate the Fisher for NGD.
rows.value: With fewer unlabeled examples, stationary risk becomes more like GD, especially with large noise.
rows.note: The text describes the Fisher estimate as expected to be closer to the sample Fisher when fewer unlabeled examples are used.
rows.check: Measures sensitivity to population-Fisher estimation data, not any listed version.

rows.subject: two-layer ReLU student
rows.size_stated: two-layer; width not stated for this experiment
rows.operation_detail: Compared additively interpolated preconditioners between GD and NGD across label noise levels.
rows.value: At certain signal-to-noise ratios, an interpolating preconditioner can achieve lower stationary risk than both GD and NGD.
rows.note: No tabulated numeric values are supplied.
rows.check: Damped population-Fisher preconditioning is not an adaptive optimizer comparison under V4. The measured outcome is regression risk.

rows.subject: two-layer ReLU student
rows.size_stated: two-layer; width not stated for this experiment
rows.operation_detail: Compared geometrically interpolated preconditioners between GD and NGD across label noise levels.
rows.value: At certain signal-to-noise ratios, an interpolating preconditioner can achieve lower stationary risk than both GD and NGD.
rows.note: No tabulated numeric values are supplied.
rows.check: Geometric full-Fisher preconditioning does not test Adam or the other adaptive-optimizer conditions in V4.

rows.subject: two-layer ReLU network
rows.stage_stated: trained toward a teacher model of the same architecture
rows.operation_detail: Compared parameter and function-output changes from initialization for GD, NGD, square-root NGD, and sample NGD.
rows.measure: Parameter-space and function-space distance from initialization; not held-out performance.
rows.baseline: GD versus NGD and sample NGD
rows.value: GD changes parameters less; NGD changes function outputs less; sample Fisher has implicit bias similar to GD.
rows.note: This measures implicit bias, not generalization error, so it cannot establish the optimizer-performance comparison.
rows.check: Parameter and function distances from initialization measure implicit bias, not held-out performance or magnitude-aware sharpness.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: tested GD and population-Fisher NGD settings
reader_labels.reason: The optimizer comparison depends on noise, misspecification and alignment: NGD has advantages in some regimes while GD is favored in others (R1–R7); interpolation can also outperform both endpoints in some noise settings (R9–R10). The study does not test the adaptive-optimizer benchmarks or tuning conditions named in V4.
